title: Part 6, Chapter 7
paragraphs: That same day, around seven in the evening, Raskolnikov was making his way to his mother's and sister's lodgings -- the rooms in Bakaleyev's house that Razumihin had found for them. The staircase led up from the street. Raskolnikov climbed with dragging steps, as though still uncertain whether to go in. But nothing would have turned him back now; his decision was made.
"Besides, it doesn't matter -- they still don't know anything," he thought, "and they're used to thinking of me as eccentric."

He was dressed appallingly: his clothes torn and dirty, soaked from a night in the rain. His face was nearly distorted from exhaustion, exposure, and the inner struggle that had consumed him for twenty-four hours. He had spent the entire previous night alone, God knows where. But he had reached a decision.

He knocked at the door. His mother opened it. Dounia was not home. Even the maid happened to be out. At first Pulcheria Alexandrovna was speechless with joy and surprise; then she took his hand and pulled him into the room.

"Here you are!" she began, faltering with happiness. "Don't be angry with me, Rodya, for greeting you so foolishly with tears. I'm laughing, not crying. Did you think I was crying? No, I'm overjoyed, but I've gotten into this silly habit of weeping. It's been like this ever since your father died -- I cry at everything. Sit down, darling, you must be tired -- I can see you are. Oh, how muddy you are!"
"I was out in the rain yesterday, Mother..." Raskolnikov began.

"No, no," Pulcheria Alexandrovna hurried to interrupt. "You thought I was going to cross-examine you the way I used to -- don't worry. I understand, I understand everything now. I've learned how things work here, and I truly see that they make more sense. I've decided once and for all: how can I expect to understand your plans or demand that you account for them? God knows what matters you're dealing with, what ideas you're working through. It's not for me to keep nudging your elbow, asking what you're thinking. But my goodness, why am I running around like a fool? I'm reading your article in the journal for the third time, Rodya. Dmitri Prokofitch brought it to me. The moment I saw it, I thought: 'There, you silly woman -- that's what he's been busy with! That's the answer! Scholars are always like this. He has new ideas in his head right now, he's thinking them over, and I just bother and upset him.' I read it, my dear, and of course there was a great deal I didn't understand, but that's only natural -- how could I?"
"Show me, Mother."

Raskolnikov took the journal and glanced at his article. As incongruous as it was with his mood and circumstances, he felt that strange, bittersweet sensation every author experiences the first time he sees himself in print; besides, he was only twenty-three. It lasted only an instant. After reading a few lines, he frowned, and his heart clenched with anguish. All the inner turmoil of the preceding months came flooding back. He flung the article on the table in disgust and anger.

"But however foolish I may be, Rodya, I can see for myself that you'll soon be one of the leading -- if not the leading -- minds in Russian thought. And they dared to think you were mad! You don't know, but they actually believed it. What wretched fools -- how could they fail to recognize genius! Even Dounia nearly believed it -- can you imagine? Your father twice submitted things to journals -- first poems, I have the manuscript and I'll show you -- and then an entire novel. I begged him to let me copy it out, and how we prayed they'd be accepted! They weren't! I was heartbroken, Rodya. But six or seven days ago I was agonizing over your food and clothes and the way you live, and now I see how foolish that was. You can achieve any position you want with your intellect and talent. No doubt you don't care about that now -- you're occupied with far more important things..."
"Dounia's not home, Mother?"

"No, Rodya. I often don't see her; she leaves me alone. Dmitri Prokofitch comes to visit me -- it's very kind of him -- and he always talks about you. He loves and respects you, dear. I'm not saying Dounia is inconsiderate. I'm not complaining. She has her ways and I have mine. She seems to have secrets lately, but I never have any secrets from you two. Of course I'm sure Dounia has far too much sense, and besides, she loves us both... but I don't know where it will all lead. You've made me so happy by coming, Rodya, but she's missed you. When she comes in, I'll tell her: 'Your brother was here while you were out. Where have you been spending your time?' You mustn't spoil me, Rodya. Come when you can, and if you can't, it doesn't matter -- I'll wait. I'll know you love me, and that's enough. I'll read what you write, I'll hear about you from everyone, and sometimes you'll come to see me. What more could I want? Here you are now, come to comfort your mother -- I can see that."
And Pulcheria Alexandrovna began to cry.

"There I go again! Don't mind my foolishness. Goodness, why am I just sitting here?" she cried, jumping up. "There's coffee and I haven't offered you any. That's the selfishness of old age. I'll get it right away!"
"Mother, don't trouble yourself. I'm going in a moment. I haven't come for that. Please listen to me."
Pulcheria Alexandrovna came up to him timidly.

"Mother, whatever happens, whatever you hear about me, whatever anyone tells you -- will you always love me as you do now?" he asked suddenly, from the fullness of his heart, as though not weighing his words.
"Rodya, Rodya, what's wrong? How can you even ask me that? And who would say anything about you? Besides, I wouldn't believe anyone -- I'd refuse to listen."

"I've come to tell you that I've always loved you, and I'm glad we're alone, glad even that Dounia isn't here," he went on with the same impulse. "I've come to say that although you will be unhappy, you must believe that your son loves you now more than himself, and that everything you thought about me -- that I was cruel and didn't care about you -- was all a mistake. I will never stop loving you. Well, that's enough. I felt I had to do this, to begin with this..."
Pulcheria Alexandrovna embraced him in silence, pressing him to her breast and weeping softly.

"I don't know what's wrong with you, Rodya," she said at last. "All this time I've been thinking we were simply boring you, but now I see that some great sorrow is waiting for you, and that's why you're so miserable. I've sensed it for a long time, Rodya. Forgive me for mentioning it. I think about it constantly and lie awake at night. Your sister was talking in her sleep all last night, talking about nothing but you. I caught some words but couldn't make them out. All morning I've had the feeling that something terrible was about to happen, that I was waiting for something -- and now it has come. Rodya, Rodya, where are you going? You're going away somewhere?"
"Yes."

"I knew it! But I could go with you, you know, if you need me. And Dounia too -- she loves you, she loves you so much. And Sofya Semyonovna could come with us, if you'd like. You see, I'm happy to think of her as a daughter now... Dmitri Prokofitch would help us all go together. But... where... where are you going?"
"Goodbye, Mother."
"What -- today?" she cried, as though losing him forever.
"I can't stay. I have to go now..."
"And I can't come with you?"
"No, but kneel down and pray to God for me. Your prayer may reach Him."
"Let me bless you and make the sign of the cross over you. That's right, that's right. Oh God, what is happening to us?"

Yes, he was glad -- very glad -- that no one else was there, that he was alone with his mother. For the first time in all those terrible months, his heart softened. He fell before her, kissed her feet, and they both wept, embracing. And she was not surprised and asked no questions this time. For days now she had sensed that something awful was happening to her son and that a terrible moment had arrived.

"Rodya, my darling, my firstborn," she said through her sobs, "now you're just like when you were small. You used to run to me like this, hug me and kiss me. When your father was alive and we were poor, just being near you was a comfort. And when I buried your father, how often we wept and embraced at his grave, just as we're doing now. And if I've been crying lately, it's because a mother's heart sensed that trouble was coming. The first time I saw you, that evening when we arrived -- I guessed everything from your eyes alone. My heart sank at once. And today, when I opened the door and looked at you, I thought the fatal hour had come. Rodya, Rodya, you're not leaving today, are you?"
"No!"
"You'll come again?"
"Yes... I'll come."
"Rodya, don't be angry -- I don't dare question you. I know I mustn't. Just tell me two words: is it far, where you're going?"
"Very far."
"What's waiting for you there? Some position, some career?"
"Whatever God sends... just pray for me." Raskolnikov moved toward the door, but she clutched at him and gazed despairingly into his eyes. Her face was twisted with fear.
"Enough, Mother," said Raskolnikov, deeply regretting that he had come.
"Not forever? It's not forever yet? You'll come again, you'll come tomorrow?"
"I will, I will. Goodbye." He tore himself away at last.

It was a warm, fresh, bright evening; the weather had cleared in the morning. Raskolnikov hurried to his lodgings. He wanted to finish everything before sunset. He wanted to meet no one until then. Going up the stairs, he noticed Nastasya rush away from the samovar to watch him intently. "Has someone come to see me?" he wondered. He had a sickening vision of Porfiry. But opening his door, he saw Dounia. She was sitting alone, plunged in deep thought, looking as though she had been waiting a long time. He stopped short in the doorway. She rose from the sofa in alarm and stood facing him. Her eyes, fixed on his, showed horror and bottomless grief. And from those eyes alone he saw at once that she knew.
"Should I come in or go away?" he asked uncertainly.
"I've been with Sofya Semyonovna all day. We were both waiting for you. We thought you'd be sure to go there."
Raskolnikov walked into the room and sank exhausted into a chair.
"I feel weak, Dounia. I'm very tired. And right now I'd like more than anything to be in control of myself."
He glanced at her with distrust.
"Where were you all night?"

"I don't remember exactly. You see, sister, I wanted to make up my mind once and for all, and several times I walked along the Neva. I remember that much. I wanted to end it all there, but... I couldn't bring myself to do it," he whispered, looking at her distrustfully again.
"Thank God! That's exactly what we were afraid of, Sofya Semyonovna and I. So you still believe in life? Thank God, thank God!"
Raskolnikov smiled bitterly.
"I don't believe. But I've just been weeping in my mother's arms. I don't believe, but I've just asked her to pray for me. I don't know how that works, Dounia. I don't understand it."
"You went to Mother's? You told her?" Dounia cried in horror. "You didn't!"

"No, I didn't tell her... not in words. But she understood a great deal. She heard you talking in your sleep. I'm certain she already half understands. Maybe I was wrong to go. I don't even know why I went. I'm a contemptible person, Dounia."
"A contemptible person who is ready to embrace suffering! You are ready, aren't you?"

"Yes. Right now. Yes, to escape the disgrace, I thought of drowning myself, Dounia. But as I stared into the water, I told myself that if I've considered myself strong until now, I shouldn't be afraid of disgrace," he said, hurrying on. "It's pride, Dounia."
"Pride, Rodya."
There was a gleam of fire in his dull eyes; he seemed glad to think he was still proud.
"You don't think, sister, that I was simply afraid of the water?" he asked, looking at her with a sinister smile.

"Oh, Rodya, stop!" Dounia cried bitterly. Silence lasted for two minutes. He sat with his eyes fixed on the floor; Dounia stood at the other end of the table, watching him in anguish. Suddenly he stood up.
"It's late. Time to go. I'm going now to turn myself in. But I don't know why I'm doing it."
Large tears rolled down her cheeks.
"You're crying, sister. But can you hold out your hand to me?"
"Did you doubt it?"
She threw her arms around him.
"By going to face your punishment, aren't you already half atoning for your crime?" she cried, holding him tight and kissing him.

"Crime? What crime?" he burst out in sudden fury. "That I killed a vile, harmful creature, a filthy old pawnbroker woman who was no use to anyone? Killing her was atonement for forty sins. She was sucking the life out of the poor. Was that a crime? I'm not thinking about it and I have no intention of atoning for it. And why does everyone keep throwing it in my face? 'A crime! A crime!' Only now do I see the full stupidity of my cowardice, now that I've decided to go through with this pointless disgrace. It's simply because I'm contemptible and have nothing in me that I've decided -- perhaps also for my own advantage, as that... Porfiry... suggested!"
"Brother, brother, what are you saying? You shed blood!" Dounia cried in despair.

"Blood that all men shed," he broke in, almost frantically, "that has flowed in torrents since the beginning of the world, that is poured out like champagne, and for which men are crowned in the Capitol and hailed as benefactors of humanity. Look more closely and you'll understand! I too wanted to do good, and I would have done hundreds, thousands of good deeds to make up for that one act of stupidity -- no, not even stupidity but clumsiness, because the idea wasn't nearly so stupid as it looks now that it's failed. Everything looks stupid when it fails. With that act of clumsiness, I only wanted to establish my independence, to take the first step, to secure the means, and then everything would have been made right by benefits beyond comparison... But I couldn't even carry out the first step, because I'm contemptible -- that's what it comes down to! And yet I refuse to see it your way. If I had succeeded, I'd have been crowned with glory, but now I'm caught in a trap."
"But that's not true, not true at all! Brother, what are you saying?"

"It's not aesthetically pleasing, I admit! I honestly can't understand why bombing people in a proper siege is considered more respectable. Fear of appearances is the first symptom of impotence. I've never seen that more clearly than I do right now, and I'm further than ever from considering what I did a crime. I've never been so strong in my convictions as I am at this moment."

Color had rushed to his pale, exhausted face. But as he uttered this last declaration, his eyes happened to meet Dounia's, and he saw such anguish in them that he couldn't help checking himself. He realized that he had, at the very least, made these two poor women miserable, that he was, at the very least, the cause of--

"Dounia, darling, if I'm guilty, forgive me -- though if I am guilty, I can't be forgiven. Goodbye! Let's not argue. It's time -- past time -- to go. Don't follow me, I beg you. There's somewhere else I need to be. But you go now and stay with Mother. I'm begging you! It's my last request. Don't leave her. I left her in a state of anxiety she can't bear -- she'll die or lose her mind. Be with her! Razumihin will be there too. I've spoken to him. Don't cry over me. I'll try to be brave and honorable for the rest of my life, even if I am a murderer. Perhaps someday I'll make a name for myself. I won't disgrace you -- you'll see. I'll prove it yet... But now, goodbye for now," he concluded hastily, noticing a strange expression on Dounia's face. "Why are you crying? Don't cry, don't cry -- we're not parting forever! Oh, wait -- I almost forgot!"

He went to the table, picked up a thick, dusty book, opened it, and took from between the pages a small watercolor portrait on ivory. It was a picture of his landlady's daughter, who had died of fever -- that strange girl who had wanted to become a nun. For a moment he gazed at the delicate, expressive face of his onetime fiancee, kissed the portrait, and handed it to Dounia.

"I used to talk to her about it, a great deal -- to her alone," he said thoughtfully. "I confided much to her heart that has since been so hideously realized. Don't worry," he turned to Dounia, "she was as much against it as you are, and I'm glad she's gone. The main thing is that everything is going to change now, to crack apart," he cried, suddenly returning to his gloom. "Everything, everything -- and am I ready for it? Do I even want it? They say suffering is necessary. What's the point of all this senseless suffering? Will I understand it any better when I'm crushed by hardship and idiocy, enfeebled like an old man after twenty years of hard labor? And what will I have to live for then? Why am I consenting to this? Oh, I knew I was contemptible when I stood looking at the Neva at dawn!"

At last they both went out. It was hard for Dounia, but she loved him. She walked away, but after fifty paces she turned to look at him once more. He was still in sight. At the corner, he too turned, and for the last time their eyes met. But noticing that she was looking at him, he waved her away with impatience, even irritation, and turned the corner sharply.

"I'm cruel, I know," he thought, immediately ashamed of his angry gesture to Dounia. "But why do they love me so much, when I don't deserve it? Oh, if only I were alone and no one loved me and I had never loved anyone! None of this would have happened. But I wonder -- in those fifteen or twenty years, will I really become so meek that I'll grovel before people and whimper at every turn that I'm a criminal? Yes, that's it -- that's exactly it -- that's what they're sending me there for, that's what they want. Look at them all running up and down the streets, every one of them a scoundrel and a criminal at heart, and worse still, an idiot. But try to get me pardoned and they'd howl with righteous indignation. Oh, how I hate them all!"

He fell to wondering by what process it could happen that he would genuinely humble himself before all of them -- humble himself out of conviction. And yet, why not? It had to be so. Wouldn't twenty years of unbroken captivity crush him completely? Water wears away stone. And why, why should he go on living after that? Why should he go now, knowing that was how it would end? It was perhaps the hundredth time he had asked himself that question since the previous evening. But still he went.
